disease_info: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, Predominantly Inattentive Presentation, is characterized by persistent patterns of inattention such as disorganization, forgetfulness, and difficulty sustaining focus, without prominent hyperactive or impulsive behaviors. Symptoms must cause clinically significant impairment in academic, occupational, or social functioning and be present for at least several months, typically with onset in childhood even if not recognized until later. In adults, it often presents as chronic problems with planning, time management, and follow-through, and may be misattributed to anxiety, depression, or personality traits like laziness or carelessness. It is distinguished from primary anxiety or mood disorders by the lifelong, cross-situational pattern of attentional difficulties that persist even when mood or anxiety symptoms are controlled.

narrative.stressor: Aamer completed his bachelor’s degree in art history with strong essays and projects, but in his final three semesters he began missing internal deadlines for independent research and applications to competitive museum internships, despite spending long solitary hours trying to work. After graduation, he moved back to Somerville expecting to transition smoothly into museum studies programs or entry-level curatorial roles, only to find himself repeatedly stalling on application packets, mismanaging timelines, and losing track of key opportunities he had meticulously bookmarked. Over the past year and eleven months, this pattern clashed sharply with his self-image as a cautious, methodical planner, leaving him unemployed despite solid credentials and creating growing tension at home as his parents questioned why he wasn’t "following through" on his plans. Frustrated that his careful schedules and organizational systems weren’t translating into completed applications or consistent work output, and noticing the gap between his capacity for deep art criticism and his inability to execute on concrete tasks, he finally agreed to see a psychiatrist at the urging of a campus mentor who suspected an underlying attentional disorder.
narrative.chief_complaint: I can plan everything out in detail, but when it’s time to actually sit down and do the work, I just can’t seem to make myself stick with it for more than a few minutes.

narrative.stressor: Robin has long relied on strict routines to succeed as a medical-surgical nurse, but about two years ago her hospital transitioned to a new EHR and more complex care pathways, demanding constant multitasking, rapid protocol changes, and independent tracking of numerous follow-up tasks. Despite her reputation for being meticulous, she began missing non-emergent but important steps—like following up on lab results or completing certain education modules—whenever the floor became busy, which led to several near-miss incidents that were caught by colleagues and supervisors. Over the past year and eleven months, she has responded by over-planning and staying late to recheck her work, yet she still finds that key tasks "slip" during hectic shifts, and she has received formal feedback about inconsistent task completion that threatens her prospects for moving into leadership roles. Feeling that her effort and worry are no longer enough to compensate, and alarmed that her reliability at work is now in question, she sought psychiatric evaluation after her nurse manager gently suggested that her difficulties with keeping track of everything might represent more than just stress.
narrative.chief_complaint: No matter how many lists and reminders I use, I keep forgetting everyday work tasks and follow-ups, and it’s starting to affect my job.

narrative.stressor: Juan has built a successful career as a healthcare operations manager by compensating for his distractibility with detailed spreadsheets and checklists, but as his network expanded and he took on more community initiatives, the sheer volume of projects began to overwhelm his usual systems. Over the last year and eleven months, he has noticed that during long strategic meetings and data review sessions, his attention drifts and he misses key points, leading to oversights in project timelines that colleagues then have to correct, even as he continues to over-commit to community events and volunteer roles. Although no single crisis occurred, a pattern of small but recurring lapses—like overlooking important emails in a chain or mis-sequencing steps in a complex rollout—started to erode his confidence and prompted quiet feedback from a trusted physician partner that he seemed "less on top of the details" than before. Concerned that his long-standing tendency to lose track of things is becoming more evident now that his responsibilities are higher-stakes, and wanting to understand why his focus slips even when he cares deeply about the work, he decided to consult a psychiatrist after reading about adult ADHD in an article on healthcare leadership performance.
narrative.chief_complaint: In long meetings or when I’m working through complex plans, my mind keeps drifting off and I miss important details even though I’m really trying to pay attention.
